name: Emeka Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What do you do at the factory?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a paver-block press. I check the concrete mix as it drops into moulds, watch the press cycle and pull a block for a strength and edge check. I have a vocational machinery certificate and have been on this line long enough to do a sound ordinary shift. I am not a specialist mechanic. The pay is low for the work, and there are only a few similar plants near home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your home situation, and how do you approach new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Hana takes sewing alterations from neighbours, and our grown sons live separately. We rent and have less than three weeks of expenses put aside; Hana’s orders change from week to week. I use AI every day to turn fault codes into questions and organise my log, then check the machine manual and ask the fitter before touching a guard. I am willing to test a new tool early if somebody supervises the moving parts. I would like to cut back shifts later, but we have not proved what income could pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the press crew a quicker order plan is fine, but a paver with a cracked corner still cannot leave the yard. The mould and compaction checks stay ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our rent gets paid while my shifts and Hana’s sewing orders both come in. The small reserve would not cover a long missed pay period. A slow change would give me more time to learn the present press properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep testing first paver blocks and recording a bad edge before another pallet is made. I would use AI to organise fault questions, then check the printed code and fitter’s answer for any actual adjustment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about how little cash we have, even with ordinary work continuing. I am interested in the tools, but first I need the pay week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you see before a weak block fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fresh paver can hide a soft corner until you lift it. I turn the first pressed block and tap its edge before a pallet goes out. The fitter taught me to look at the mould fill as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust an AI repair instruction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read it as a question, not a command. I compare the fault code with the printed manual, then have the fitter verify a guard or pressure adjustment. I cannot let a phone sign off a press.

say: I would **keep** paver-edge and compaction checks despite faster office orders.
A **cracked** block cannot be sent out as good stock.
think: Our **wages** pay rent only while my shifts and sewing orders continue.
**Less** than three weeks saved leaves us exposed.
do: **Keep** testing first pavers before pallets are made.
**Use** AI for fault questions while checking manual and fitter before adjustments.
feel: **Uneasy** about thin cash despite continued familiar paid work.
S0.quote: I turn the first pressed block and tap its edge before a pallet goes out.
fieldNote: **Emeka** is an experienced average-skill paver-press operator with a vocational machinery certificate and lower pay.
He and **alterations** worker wife Hana rent, have grown sons and less than three weeks of expenses saved.
He **uses** AI every day for fault questions but verifies all physical adjustments with manual and fitter.

steps.text: Keep testing first pressed pavers and verifying machine adjustments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor to separate the office order changes from any robot that lifts the wet pavers. I would like to see the robot work a whole shift with guards and the reject count visible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loader could eventually take hands off the mould line, including some of my hours. I am quick with a new screen, but that will not keep a position open if the roster shrinks. Less than three weeks saved gives us little time to find other work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a guarded full-shift loader trial and compare broken edges with our usual tally. If the plant offers paid instruction on a new AI quality screen, I would learn it and test its reject marks against physical blocks. I would apply for a posted local quality job only if its net wage after travel and hours cover rent and fit Hana’s variable work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a cut to my hours, even while I want to try the screen. I would not enter a robot paver-stacker cell just because I watched it move blocks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the robot controls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the plant offers a funded paid recognised practical place with a fitter, safe stops and isolation, and time to practise on a guarded cell. I would be glad to learn it early. I would not reach past the guard to prove enthusiasm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the quality role never appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the present press wage and check posted operator jobs at the few nearby plants. I would count travel cost and shift hours against rent before applying. We cannot use a rumour to pay a bill.

say: I would **ask** for a full guarded trial with reject counts.
**Office** orders change before physical robot lifting.
think: A **later** loader may cut my press hours.
A **quick** new screen skill cannot replace a lost wage.
do: Request **guarded robot trial**; accept offered recognised funded paid practice only with a fitter, safe stops and lockout.
**Learn** offered AI quality screen on paid time against physical blocks.
Apply for **posted quality work** or operator fallback only if net pay after travel and shifts cover rent.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, eager for safe proven learning.
S1.quote: I would not enter a robot paver-stacker cell just because I watched it move blocks.
fieldNote: **Emeka** wants an observed robot trial; operation requires a separate offered funded paid recognised safe-practice place.
He would **actually** learn an AI quality screen only with offered paid instruction and physical cross-checks.
A **quality** application and fallback search each need postings, adequate wages after travel and workable shifts.

steps.text: Request full guarded loader trial and compare broken-edge rejects
Learn offered AI quality screen on paid time with physical block checks
Apply for posted quality work or operator fallback if net pay/hours after travel cover rent
Accept offered funded paid recognised robot practice with fitter, safe stops and lockout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew AGI can handle orders in 2028, while capable robots mixing, pressing and stacking pavers around 2031 may remove floor shifts. The plant needs to put its plans and training terms in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a sharp cut to press hours once a robot can manage a complete run. I will be 63 then. Hana’s sewing orders alone would not meet rent, and our little reserve would disappear quickly; I would be awake worrying about the next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would stop the planned kitchen cupboard replacement and list rent, power and food first. I would ask the landlord about an arrangement before a missed payment and the plant for written redeployment terms. I would apply for a posted local materials-checking job only with paid supervised safety training and net pay after travel and hours that cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about the likely loss of my press wage. Being willing to learn cannot feed us during a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would AI use qualify you for materials checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can organise a report, but I do not yet know safe robot isolation or every material test. I would need an offered paid practical course and a real posted vacancy. My daily AI use does not make me a trained materials inspector.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sons support you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They could help if they offered, but I will not put their wages in our budget. They have their own homes. I would count written work terms and rent arrangements first.

say: I would **ask** for written plans before capable paver robots around 2031.
2028 **AGI** order changes come about three years earlier.
think: I **expect** a major loss of paid paver-press hours at 63.
**Thin** savings and variable sewing income cannot carry rent alone.
do: **Cancel** cupboard replacement and list household bills.
**Ask** landlord about rent terms and plant about redeployment.
**Apply** for posted materials work only with paid safety training and bill-covering net pay and hours.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and awake over next month rent.
S2.quote: My daily AI use does not make me a trained materials inspector.
fieldNote: **Emeka** expects paver-floor risk around 2031, after AGI handles office orders in 2028.
**Daily** AI use does not establish physical inspection or robot safety skill.
His **under-three-week** reserve and variable partner earnings make a major press-hour cut frightening.

steps.text: Cancel planned cupboard replacement and list essential bills
Ask landlord about arrangement before missed rent
Ask plant for written redeployment terms
Apply for posted materials work with paid safety training bill-covering net pay after travel and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the factory five years is enough to offer a real paid apprenticeship to operators, not just mechanics. AGI changes ordering in 2031 and capable paver robots arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 66 by the robot date. I know the press and use AI daily, but neither teaches me to isolate a moving stacker. I would like the chance to keep earning if retirement figures are short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol in an offered recognised materials-and-robot-safety course only if funded on paid hours with supervised isolation, concrete-test practice and a timetable I can attend. After qualifying, I would apply for a posted local materials job only if its net pay after travel and shift cover rent. If no paid place comes, I would keep the press wage and search posted nearby concrete jobs with enough pay and workable hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about having a real place and job by 66, but I would learn the controls eagerly with a fitter there. An unpaid robot-safety course would make our rent problem worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of the course matters most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise stopping the stacker, proving it cannot move and then checking a test block with the instructor. A diagram is useful, but I need repeated safe work on paid time. I would ask the fitter to sign the practical check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop paid shifts at 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Hana and I get written income figures that meet rent, food and other costs. We have not counted on a pension amount. If the figures fall short, I must keep earning.

say: I would **ask** for an offered paid practical course before 2034.
**AGI** orders arrive in 2031 before paver robots.
think: At 66, **press** experience and daily AI use do not prove robot isolation.
**Retirement** remains conditional on actual rent-covering income.
do: **Enrol** in offered funded paid recognised course with supervised isolation concrete tests and workable hours.
**Apply** after course for posted materials job only with rent-covering net pay after travel and shifts.
If **no** paid course, seek posted concrete jobs with sufficient wage and hours.
feel: **Anxious** about actual places, eager for safe paid practice.
S3.quote: An unpaid robot-safety course would make our rent problem worse.
fieldNote: **Emeka** would enrol only in an offered recognised funded paid course with supervised robot isolation and concrete-test practice.
He **separately** applies for a posted materials job only with net pay after travel and workable hours covering rent.
**Without** a course, he keeps the present wage and checks posted nearby concrete jobs.

steps.text: Enrol in offered funded paid recognised course with supervised isolation concrete tests and workable hours
Apply after qualification for posted materials job only with rent-covering net pay after travel and shifts
Seek posted concrete work if no course and wages and hours suffice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my sons that ten years should let us put retirement costs and any apprenticeship terms on paper. AGI changes orders in 2036, and capable robots reach the paver press around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 68 at the first date and 71 when robots arrive. We might have stopped shifts if real income covers rent, but we do not know that now. If I still need work, the plant must offer a safe paid route rather than ask me to work into my seventies by default.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written retirement-income and household-cost estimates. If wages are still needed, I would take an offered recognised funded paid course with supervised stacker isolation on attendable hours, then apply for a posted local materials job only if net pay after travel and shifts cover rent. Without a safe paid place, I would search posted concrete or warehouse jobs with bill-covering wages and workable hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the income question, but I like having enough time to get answers. The longer warning helps only if the training offer and job are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach AI use to other operators?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I show a coworker how I turn a fault code into a question for the fitter, then compare it with the manual. I would keep doing that while I have a shift. I would not claim the AI answer is a safety sign-off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you stop working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana and I would compare written expected income with rent, food and health costs first. If it covers those, we may choose to stop full shifts. If it does not, I will seek safe paid work rather than assume an age settles it.

say: I would **ask** for retirement figures and written paid-apprenticeship terms.
2036 **order** AI precedes hands-on paver robots around 2039.
think: At 68 in 2036 I **may** have stopped shifts if income covers rent.
At 71 **near** 2039 any factory work depends on actual figures.
do: **Request** written retirement income and cost estimates.
If **work** remains necessary, take offered funded paid safe course on attendable hours.
**After** course, apply for posted materials job only with rent-covering net pay and shifts.
feel: **Uneasy** about unknown retirement income, interested in real training terms.
S4.quote: I would not claim the AI answer is a safety sign-off.
fieldNote: **Emeka** assumes neither a pension payment nor employment at 71; written income and cost figures decide.
If **wages** are still needed, training requires an offered recognised funded paid place with supervised stacker safety.
A **posted** materials job must cover rent after travel, while no-course fallback checks concrete or warehouse work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because capable paver robots could cut my press hours around 2031 with less than three weeks saved. A funded paid safe course and a posted job covering rent would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I use AI every day, and I would teach a new operator to check it against the manual. My daily AI use does not make me a trained materials inspector.

portrait: **Emeka** Fischer, 58, is an experienced average-skill paver-press operator with a vocational machinery certificate.
He and **alterations** worker wife Hana rent, have grown sons and less than three weeks saved on lower operator pay.
He **uses** AI every day for fault questions, then verifies physical settings with manual and fitter.
**Curious** and willing to try new tools, he still faces scarce nearby jobs and serious wage risk.
**Retirement** needs actual income figures; any training and materials job must be offered, paid, safe and bill covering.
biggestWorry: **Capable** robots around 2031 could cut his paver-press shifts with less than three weeks saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Offer** funded paid supervised robot training and posted local jobs with net wages and hours covering rent.
